title: Evolution from Monolith → Microservices
subtitle: Modular monoliths, bounded contexts, the Strangler Fig pattern, and zero-downtime database extraction.
keyTakeaways: Microservices primarily solve organizational scaling challenges (hundreds of engineers blocked by shared deployment pipelines and merge conflicts), not technical performance: start with a well-factored Modular Monolith.
Never allow multiple microservices to query the same physical database tables: decompose the shared database before or alongside service extraction using Change Data Capture (CDC) or dual-writing.
Migrate iteratively using the Strangler Fig pattern and shadow traffic verification at the API Gateway rather than attempting a high-risk big-bang rewrite.

sections.heading: Decomposition Triggers and Avoiding the Distributed Monolith
sections.body: Splitting a monolith prematurely often results in a "Distributed Monolith"—a system that suffers from all the network latency, serialization overhead, and partial failure modes of microservices while retaining the tight coupling and release lockstep of the original monolith.
bullets: Organizational scaling triggers: Decompose a monolith when teams spend more time resolving merge conflicts, waiting in deployment queues, and coordinating cross-team releases than writing software. If a single team manages the system, a modular monolith is almost always faster to develop and easier to operate.

Domain-Driven Design (DDD) bounded contexts: Draw service boundaries around business domains with independent lifecycles (e.g., Billing, Inventory, Authentication) rather than technical layers (e.g., "data access service" vs "UI service").

Strict modular boundaries first: Enforce strict in-process API boundaries within the monolith using package-private visibility and architectural linter checks before breaking code out into separate networked repositories.

sections.heading: The Zero-Downtime Database Decomposition Playbook
sections.body: Extracting application code into a new microservice is relatively straightforward; separating a 10 TB shared database with dozens of foreign keys and cross-table joins without downtime is where migrations succeed or fail.
bullets: Step 1: Eliminate database joins in application code: Refactor monolithic queries that join across domain boundaries into two separate queries, combining the data in the application layer.
Step 2: Dual-writing or Change Data Capture (CDC): Stream mutations from the monolith's database to the new service's database using Debezium or Kafka to maintain real-time synchronization.
Step 3: Backfill historical data: Run background migration scripts to copy historical records into the new database without locking live transactional tables.
Step 4: Shadow reading and validation: The API Gateway routes reads to both the monolith and the new service asynchronously, comparing results to ensure 100% data and behavior consistency.
Step 5: Cutover and deprecation: Shift primary write traffic to the new service, redirect remaining monolith reads to the new service's API, and decommission the old monolithic tables.

tradeOffs.pros: Zero network serialization latency; single deployment pipeline; simple ACID transactions and refactoring.
tradeOffs.cons: Single blast radius for process crashes; deployment coordination required as engineering team grows past 50-100 devs.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Early-stage platforms, startups, and mid-sized engineering teams prioritizing feature velocity.

tradeOffs.pros: Independent team deployment autonomy; tailored technology stacks; bounded blast radius for component crashes.
tradeOffs.cons: High operational complexity (distributed tracing, eventual consistency, network latency, cross-service debugging).
tradeOffs.bestFor: Large engineering organizations (100+ developers) with distinct, autonomous product teams.

interviewTip: When an interviewer asks how to migrate a monolith to microservices, emphasize that code extraction is the easy part—the true challenge is database decomposition. Walk through the 5-step playbook: eliminating joins, CDC streaming, backfilling, shadow reading, and safe traffic cutover.
